questions.question: A separating hyperplane of nonempty $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is a set $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$ with $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b$ on $V_1$ and $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\geq b$ on $V_2$ (or the reverse). Why does the definition require $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$?
options: With $\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{0}$ the two inequalities could only hold if $V_1$ and $V_2$ were the same set.
With $\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{0}$ the set $H$ would pass through the origin, which a separating hyperplane must avoid.
With $\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{0}$ and $b=0$ both inequalities hold for any two sets, and $H$ is all of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
With $\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{0}$ no value of $b$ satisfies both inequalities, so no pair of sets could be separated.

questions.question: For nonempty $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and a hyperplane $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$ with $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, which description in terms of halfspaces says exactly that $H$ is a separating hyperplane of $V_1$ and $V_2$?
options: One set lies in a closed halfspace bounded by $H$ and the other set lies in the opposite closed halfspace.
One set lies in an open halfspace bounded by $H$ and the other set lies in the opposite open halfspace.
Both sets lie in the same closed halfspace bounded by $H$, and each of the two sets touches $H$.
The two sets lie in opposite closed halfspaces bounded by $H$, and $H$ contains no point of either set.

questions.question: A separating hyperplane $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$ of nonempty $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ may have $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b$ on $V_1$ and $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\geq b$ on $V_2$, or the same with the inequalities interchanged. Why is it natural to allow both orders?
options: The interchanged inequalities describe a different hyperplane, parallel to $H$ and on the far side of both sets.
The interchanged order is needed only for $b<0$, because dividing by a negative $b$ flips both inequalities.
The interchanged order is needed only when $V_1$ and $V_2$ have a common point lying on the hyperplane $H$.
The pair $(-\boldsymbol{a},-b)$ describes the same set $H$ and turns one order of the inequalities into the other.

questions.question: Nonempty sets $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ have a common point $\boldsymbol{p}\in V_1\cap V_2$, and $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$ with $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ is a separating hyperplane of $V_1$ and $V_2$. What follows about $\boldsymbol{p}$?
options: $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}<b$, so $\boldsymbol{p}$ lies strictly on the side of whichever set is below $H$.
$\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}=b$, so the common point $\boldsymbol{p}$ lies on the hyperplane $H$ itself.
$\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}=0$, so the normal vector $\boldsymbol{a}$ is orthogonal to the point $\boldsymbol{p}$.
$\boldsymbol{p}$ is the only common point, since $H$ can meet each of the two sets in one point only.

questions.question: The hyperplane $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$, $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, separates nonempty $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b$ on $V_1$ and $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\geq b$ on $V_2$. Starting at a point $\boldsymbol{x}_0\in H$, where does a step in the direction of $\boldsymbol{a}$ lead?
options: Into the halfspace $\{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b\}$ of $V_1$, since a normal vector points back at the set below.
Along $H$ itself, since the normal vector $\boldsymbol{a}$ is parallel to the hyperplane that it determines.
Into the halfspace $\{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\geq b\}$ of $V_2$, as $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ grows along it.
Towards $V_1$ when $b>0$ and towards $V_2$ when $b<0$, since the sign of $b$ fixes the orientation.

questions.question: Let $V_1=\{(0,0),(1,2),(2,0)\}$ and $V_2=\{(3,2),(2,3),(4,1)\}$ be finite sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which line is a separating hyperplane of $V_1$ and $V_2$?
In $\mathbb{R}^3$, let $V_1=\{(0,0,0)\}$ and $V_2=\{(0,0,2)\}$. Which set is a separating hyperplane of $V_1$ and $V_2$?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x_1=0,\ x_2=0\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x_3=1,\ x_1=0\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x_1+x_2=1\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x_1+x_3=1\}$

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$ (so $n=1$) a hyperplane is a set $\{x\colon ax=b\}$ with $a\neq0$. Which sets are the separating hyperplanes of the intervals $V_1=[-1,2]$ and $V_2=[3,5]$?
options: The one-point sets $\{c\}$ with $2\leq c\leq3$, one for each such $c$.
The interval $[2,3]$, which is the gap between the two sets.
Only points strictly inside the gap: the sets $\{c\}$ with $2<c<3$.
Only the two one-point sets $\{2\}$ and $\{3\}$, which touch the sets.

questions.question: Let $V_1=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+2x_2\leq2\}$, a closed halfspace, and $V_2=\{(4,1)\}$. Which line is a separating hyperplane of $V_1$ and $V_2$?
Let $V_1$ be the triangle with corners $(0,0)$, $(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$, and let $V_2=\{(1,1)\}$. Which line is a separating hyperplane of $V_1$ and $V_2$?

A hyperplane $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$, $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, separates two nonempty finite sets $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$. Does $H$ also separate the convex hulls $\operatorname{Conv}(V_1)$ and $\operatorname{Conv}(V_2)$?
options: Only when $\operatorname{Conv}(V_1)$ and $\operatorname{Conv}(V_2)$ are disjoint; otherwise another hyperplane is needed.
Yes: each closed halfspace is convex, so it contains the convex hull of any subset of it.
Not in general: the convex hulls contain new points, which may land on the wrong side of $H$.
Yes, but only when neither $V_1$ nor $V_2$ has a point lying on the hyperplane $H$ itself.

questions.question: For nonempty sets $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ that are not assumed to be convex, how is the condition $V_1\cap V_2=\varnothing$ related to the existence of a separating hyperplane of $V_1$ and $V_2$?
options: Disjointness is neither required for, nor enough to guarantee, a separating hyperplane.
Separated sets are always disjoint, but disjoint sets need not be separable.
Disjoint sets can always be separated, but separated sets may overlap.
Two such sets can be separated by a hyperplane exactly when they are disjoint.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$, and nonempty $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfy $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b$ on $V_1$ and $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq b$ on $V_2$. Which statement holds for every $\boldsymbol{z}=\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}$ ($\boldsymbol{x}\in V_1$, $\boldsymbol{y}\in V_2$), for all such $V_1$, $V_2$, $b$?
options: $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{z}\leq b$, the same bound that holds on the set $V_1$.
$\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{z}\geq0$, since $\boldsymbol{y}$ lies on the side of larger values.
$\boldsymbol{z}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, since two separated sets have no point in common.
$\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{z}\leq0$, so the differences lie in a halfspace bounded through $\boldsymbol{0}$.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ let $V_1=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon(x_1+1)^2+x_2^2<1\}$ and $V_2=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon(x_1-1)^2+x_2^2<1\}$, two disjoint open discs whose closures share the point $(0,0)$. Which statement about a separating hyperplane of $V_1$ and $V_2$ is correct?
options: The line $x_2=0$ separates them, as it joins the centres $(-1,0)$ and $(1,0)$.
The line $x_1+x_2=0$ separates them, as it passes through the point $(0,0)$.
The line $x_1=0$ separates them, as it is perpendicular to the line of centres.
No line separates them, as the closures of the two discs share the point $(0,0)$.

questions.question: The region on or above the parabola $x_2=x_1^2$, $V_1=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_2\geq x_1^2\}$, is to be separated from the single point $(2,1)$. Which line is a separating hyperplane of $V_1$ and $\{(2,1)\}$?
Let $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1^2+x_2^2=1\}$ be the unit circle, which is not convex, and $V_2=\{(3,0)\}$. Which statement about a separating hyperplane of $S$ and $V_2$ is correct?
options: The line $x_1+x_2=2$ separates them, so convexity of $S$ is not needed here.
The line $x_1+x_2=1$ separates them, since $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ lie on it.
The line $x_1=1$ does not separate them, because it touches $S$ at $(1,0)$.
No line separates them, because the unit circle $S$ is not a convex set.

questions.question: Nonempty sets $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ have three common points that do not lie on one line. What can be said about separating hyperplanes of $V_1$ and $V_2$?
options: Exactly one exists, because the three common points pin down the separating line.
One exists whenever $V_1$ and $V_2$ are both convex, by separation of convex sets.
Every line through at least one of the three common points separates the two sets.
None exists, because a separating line would have to contain all three points.

questions.question: For nonempty $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, which condition is equivalent to the existence of a separating hyperplane of $V_1$ and $V_2$?
options: For every $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$: $\sup_{\boldsymbol{x}\in V_1}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\inf_{\boldsymbol{y}\in V_2}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$.
For some $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$: $\sup_{\boldsymbol{x}\in V_1}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\inf_{\boldsymbol{y}\in V_2}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$.
For some $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$: $\sup_{\boldsymbol{x}\in V_1}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}<\inf_{\boldsymbol{y}\in V_2}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$.
For some $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$: $\inf_{\boldsymbol{x}\in V_1}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\sup_{\boldsymbol{y}\in V_2}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$.

questions.question: Let $V_1=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+2x_2\leq4,\ 2x_1-x_2\leq3,\ -x_1\leq0\}$ and $V_2=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon -x_1-2x_2\leq-4,\ -3x_1+x_2\leq-5,\ x_2\leq3\}$, which share the point $\boldsymbol{p}=(2,1)$. Which line is a separating hyperplane of $V_1$ and $V_2$?
In $\mathbb{R}^2$, let $V_1=\{(0,0),(2,0)\}$ and $V_2=\{(1,0)\}$. Which statement correctly identifies a separating hyperplane of $V_1$ and $V_2$?
options: The line $x_1=1$, which passes through the single point of $V_2$.
The line $x_2=1$, which runs parallel to the line holding all points.
The line $x_2=0$, which contains all three points of the two sets.
No line works, since $(1,0)$ lies between the two points of $V_1$.
